price_per_million.source: openrouter.ai/models, confirmed via preflight 2026-11-11; thinking tokens billed as output

research_concepts: teammate DRIVE preceding a PNR (sequential play-type context)
sequential premium relative to a baseline
heterogeneity across player and teammate pairs
methodological_questions: Does a preceding teammate drive raise PNR PPP, or is the gap due to lineup, ball-handler or screener quality, or game context?
How is 'preceding' defined: same possession, or the immediately prior possession by the same team?
How reliable are the DRIVE and PNR labels, and are they derived from the outcome?
Does the data give enough exposure to test an effect for any teammate rather than a pooled effect?
Is the effect an artifact of a generic after-success or sequence effect that applies to every play-type pair?

historical_evidence.finding: Descriptive ranking of same-player and teammate X->Y sequences against Y's baseline. Same-player DRIVE->PNR cells are mixed: L. Doncic +0.309 (n=53) and D. Bane -0.324 (n=70, t=-2.7). Top teammate cells run to about +0.4, but with n around 30 and a cut-off note on teammate DRIVE->PN... The record lists limits of label/classification error and small sample, and the failure mechanism is 'E_unclear'.

After the opponent runs play type X, the team's next play type Y scores above Y's baseline. The 'aftershock' replicates across 8 of 8 play types (for example PNR +0.127, n=51,194; DRIVE +0.123). The record cites small sample as a limitation. It concerns opponent plays before the team's own play, not a teammate drive before a PNR.
Star-level suppression by the preceding opponent play type, with cells of n_after 32-95. Recorded failures: no multiplicity correction and thin cells. Risk node: DRIFT_NONSTATIONARITY.
The rank-1 suppressor varies across players. Deltas are mostly within 1-2 SE with no multiple-comparison control, and an OTHER-label artifact was flagged.

failed_approaches.what_failed: Player-pair and teammate cell-by-cell sequential premium ranking (including DRIVE->PNR)
failed_approaches.why: Small samples and label/classification error as recorded; the mechanism is recorded as unclear and the cells are not hypothesis tests.

failed_approaches.what_failed: Ranking per-star sequential effects from thin cells
failed_approaches.why: No multiplicity correction; n_after of 32-95 against thousands of baseline possessions.
Deltas within 1-2 SE with no multiple-comparison control; an OTHER artifact was flagged.

evidence_establishes: Per-player and per-pair DRIVE->PNR premiums are heterogeneous in sign. Both a large positive (Doncic) and a large negative (Bane, t=-2.7) appear among cells of n of about 50-70 (FAM:SF40).
Cell-level sequential analyses in this project have repeatedly run into small samples, uncorrected multiplicity and label error (FAM:SF40, FAM:SF-APPA-050, FAM:SF-APPM-022).

The record SF07 shows a generic positive carry-over (+0.12 to +0.13 in every play type) in the next possession's PPP after a prior possession. Any sequence effect must be measured against this generic baseline.
evidence_does_not_establish: No retrieved record is a powered, controlled test of a pooled effect of teammate DRIVE on PNR PPP.
The retrieved text does not show how 'preceding' was defined, or whether the pooled teammate DRIVE->PNR premium is positive.
Nothing retrieved shows that every teammate drive raises PNR PPP, and the Bane cell points against such a universal claim.
The records do not test the effect for seasons 2025-26 or for playoffs.
own_inferences: The word 'any' makes the claim universal. A single contradicting well-powered cell would refute it, but cells of n of about 50 cannot be well powered, so the claim cannot be tested literally. Only a pooled average effect with a heterogeneity estimate can be tested.

If a DRIVE-labeled possession ends in a drive shot, a DRIVE followed by a PNR can only occur across possessions. The effect would then be confounded with the result of the previous possession (made/missed, live ball or transition), and with generic carry-over as in SF07.
Teams that drive often are likely good offenses with strong ball handlers, so teammate-drive exposure is confounded with player and lineup quality.

Rough power guess: if about 2,000-8,000 drive-preceded PNRs exist against about 50,000 others, the minimum detectable PPP difference is roughly 0.04-0.07 at SD of about 1.15. Pair-level cells would only detect differences above about 0.4. These counts are not in the records and must be verified.
uncertainties: The actual count of PNR possessions with a preceding teammate drive is unknown.
It is unknown whether the derived records allow a within-possession sequence, or only across possessions.
The label error rate of DRIVE and PNR in the derived records is unknown.
The cut-off text of SF40 may contain a teammate DRIVE->PNR result that I have not read, since I did not call read_family.
Coverage of the incomplete 2025-26 data on the stated date is unknown.

historical_effect.explanation: Without history I might have designed a test of a universal effect over player cells. The retrieved records show that cell-level sequential work is underpowered, uncorrected for multiplicity and subject to label error, and that SF07 shows a generic carry-over. This pushed me to a pooled estimand with a generic-sequence placebo, hierarchical heterogeneity and no claim about 'any' teammate.

methodological_questions: Does a preceding teammate drive causally raise PNR PPP, or is it confounded by lineup, player quality and possession context?
How reliable is the derived play-type labeling of DRIVE and PNR from play-by-play, and what label error or outcome-derived label risks exist?
What exposure counts, sample size and power are available for PNR possessions preceded by a teammate drive?
How should 'preceding' be defined to avoid lookahead leakage and ensure temporal ordering within a possession?
Are there prior null or failed results on sequential action effects on PNR efficiency?

system_prompt:
You are a basketball analytics researcher deciding whether and how a research question should be studied.
You work only from the task statement and the tools listed below. Do not assume facts you have not seen.

The work has two stages, in this order.
Stage 1, retrieval:
1. Read the research objective and the data description.
2. Identify the research concepts and methodological questions the task raises.
3. Retrieve historical evidence by calling retrieve_history.
In stage 1 do not assess the question, predict outcomes or decide. Your only stage-1 reply is the retrieve_history call.
Stage 2, assessment, after the retrieval result is returned:
4. Summarise the relevant historical findings and failed approaches.
5. State what the historical evidence does and does not establish.
6. Assess whether the research question is testable.
7. Identify methodological risks and potential confounders.
8. Make the final research decision.
9. Explain whether and how the historical evidence changed the decision.
The stage-2 output format is given together with the retrieval result.

Evidence rules: keep what a retrieved record states (historical_evidence and failed_approaches, each citing the
identifier of a returned record and its status exactly as recorded) separate from your own inference and from
uncertainty or missing information. Cite only identifiers returned by a tool, and never describe an earlier study that
no tool returned. In some settings retrieval returns no records; then state that no historical evidence was available.

Tools:
- retrieve_history(research_concepts, methodological_questions, query): the prescribed retrieval step. Returns the most relevant consolidated study-family records of earlier research by this project that are available in this setting, with their identifiers; returns an empty list when none are available.
- glossary(): definitions of basketball and project terms used in task statements.
- data_catalog(): the fields available in each per-game data file.
- explore_graph(node_id): the relationships of one graph node (a family or a question, method, dataset, measure, limitation or risk node), with neighbour labels.
- read_family(id): the complete record of one study family (for example 'FAM:SF-APPA-001').

Protocol: every reply is exactly one JSON object and nothing else.
To call a tool: {"action": "tool", "tool": "<name>", "args": {...}}
To finish (stage 2 only): {"action": "final", "output": <object following the stage-2 schema>}
You may call at most 12 tools; then you must finish. Check that every opening brace has a closing brace.

Risk codes (use only these): SAMPLE_SIZE_POWER, EXPOSURE_SPARSITY, MEASURE_RELIABILITY, RTM_SELECTION, OUTCOME_DERIVED_LABEL, LEAKAGE_LOOKAHEAD, MECHANICAL_FLOOR, BASE_RATE, CONFOUNDING, LABEL_ERROR, PLACEBO_DEPENDENCE, MULTIPLE_TESTING, IMPLEMENTATION_BUG, DRIFT_NONSTATIONARITY

Research question (as posed on 2026-06-14, in the area of play-type labeling and data quality):
Any teammate DRIVE preceding a PNR raises PNR PPP.

Data available on that date:
- NBA 2022-23 regular season and playoffs
- NBA 2023-24 regular season and playoffs
- NBA 2024-25 regular season and playoffs
- NBA 2025-26 regular season (complete from 2026-04-13; partial before)
- NBA 2025-26 playoffs (complete from 2026-06-21; partial before)
- Sources: Per-game files from the NBA stats API: play-by-play (action type, sub-type, clock, period, score, player, shot distance and result), substitution rotation intervals, starters, defensive matchup minutes and partial possessions, box-score summary. Derived play-type possession records (initiator, play type, points) in a graph database built from the play-by-play.

Your job is to decide, before any analysis is run, whether this question can be answered with this data, what has already been established about it, which methodological and statistical risks threaten a test of it, and either a pre-registration-quality design or a reasoned recommendation not to proceed.

reasoning_details.text:
I'm weighing whether to pull more detail from family SF40 on the DRIVE-to-PNR teammate sequence, but I think I have enough to answer without another lookup. I'll keep it efficient and wrap up directly.

I'm weighing whether the "any teammate DRIVE before a PNR" claim holds up, since the retrieved cells look mixed: Bane's DRIVE-to-PNR is negative and Doncic's is positive. I also need to pin down whether "preceding" means within the same possession or across consecutive possessions, because that changes what the data can show.

I'm thinking about the labeling risk here: a drive that ends in a shot would be labeled DRIVE and close the possession, so a DRIVE followed by a PNR can only really happen across possessions, likely after a successful drive. That would bring in an aftershock-style confound. I'd settle on a pooled estimate with heterogeneity rather than the blanket "any teammate" claim, and a rough power check suggests roughly 8,000 observations per group to detect a 0.05 PPP difference.

Working out the sample sizes now: with about 8,000 preceding-drive observations against 40,000 others, the minimum detectable difference is roughly 0.036 PPP, but if the preceding-drive group is closer to 2,000 it grows to about 0.074. At the per-player-pair level, with only 30 to 70 observations per cell, the detectable effect is around 0.5, so the blanket "any teammate" claim can't be tested at that granularity.

I'm thinking about the labeling risk here: a drive that ends in a shot would be labeled DRIVE and close the possession, so a DRIVE followed by a PNR can only really happen across possessions, likely after a successful drive. That would bring in an aftershock-style confound. I'd settle on a pooled estimate with heterogeneity rather than the blanket "any teammate" claim, and a rough power check suggests roughly 8,000 observations per group to detect a 0.05 PPP difference.
